**A separate draft model is not the only way to propose future tokens.** Medusa adds prediction heads that propose multiple future-token candidates from a shared backbone. EAGLE-style methods use learned feature-level prediction to construct proposals efficiently. Both try to reduce the serial cost of ordinary target-only decoding, but their architecture and verification choices differ. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15077)

**Think of shared preparation versus a second worker.** A standalone draft model maintains its own weights and computation path. Extra heads can reuse information already computed by the target backbone, potentially reducing duplicate work. However, they add training, memory, candidate-tree construction, and verification complexity.

A proposal tree can contain several plausible next-token paths. A specially masked target pass evaluates these candidate paths without allowing one branch to see another branch's tokens. Accepted tokens then extend the real sequence; rejected branches are discarded.

**Keep distributional claims tied to the algorithm.** Producing several candidates at once does not automatically preserve the original target distribution. Exact speculative sampling requires the appropriate proposal probabilities and rejection/residual procedure. Greedy or heuristic acceptance can instead define a different decoding behavior. State which setting is being discussed before promising identical outputs or quality.

Compare acceptance depth, draft/head overhead, target verification cost, and end-to-end latency at realistic batch sizes. Multi-token proposals are most useful when they save more expensive serial work than they introduce. Report performance on the tasks and model versions actually tested, because proposal quality can change substantially under domain shift or model updates.

**Technical details and references.**

A standalone draft model has its own parameters and autoregressive state. Medusa attaches multiple prediction heads to target-model hidden states, creating candidate continuation trees that can be verified with tree-structured attention. EAGLE drafts using target features and token information, rather than independently modeling only token history. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15077)

These approaches reduce drafting overhead and share information with the target, but require extra training and architecture support. Their speedup depends on how many proposed tokens survive verification relative to proposal and verification cost.

Do not infer distributional exactness solely from “multi-head decoding.” Exact speculative sampling needs the appropriate proposal probabilities and rejection/residual rule; some practical acceptance modes trade exactness for speed. Compare acceptance rate, quality, latency, and memory under the actual decoding configuration. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)
